findings.title: DBML — construct expressiveness, MUST-criteria, licence, and generation profile
findings.summary:
Ten advanced constructs, each with a verdict drawn from the DBML language reference (docs.md), corroborated where noted by the CLI source and export golden-file tests:
- Composite primary keys: expressible — `(col1, col2) [pk]` inside an `indexes{}` block.
- JSON payload columns: expressible — column type is free text passed through to the target dialect (e.g. `json`/`jsonb`).
- Enumerated string domains: expressible — dedicated `enum` block.
- Several self-referencing FKs on one table: expressible — the Ref/relationship grammar has no rule barring the same table on both sides; corroborated only by a two-table (not three-on-one) parser test fixture, so the 'three at once' case for TASK_INSTANCE is inferred, not directly demonstrated.
- Nullable FKs: expressible — column `null`/`not null` (default null) plus a `?` optional-side relationship modifier.
- Multi-column UNIQUE: expressible — the same `indexes{}` block, `[unique]` setting on a parenthesized column tuple.
- One-to-zero-or-one: expressible — the one-to-one operator `-` combined with the documented `?` optional-side modifier (no worked `-?` example, but a direct rule application).
- Value constraint beyond type: expressible — a dedicated `checks{}` block and column-level `check:` setting; the constraint expression itself is opaque, dialect-specific SQL text that DBML does not parse.
- Several logical schemas in one database: expressible — an arbitrary `schema_name` prefix on any table/enum/relationship, with no documented limit on count.
- Cross-cutting `domain_id`-on-every-table convention: not-expressible by any built-in DBML mechanism; would require an external script against `@dbml/core`'s parsed model.

MUST criteria: (1) plain-text/version-controlled/product-neutral — pass; the dialect choice is deferred to `dbml2sql`'s target flag, not baked into the source. (2) Validator exits non-zero on malformed input — fail: direct reading of `@dbml/cli`'s `export.ts` and `bin/dbml2sql.js` found no `process.exit` call on a `CompilerError`; `hasErrors` is computed but only suppresses a success message, so the process exits 0 by default even after logging errors. (3) SVG/PNG from an ephemeral Docker container with zero local install — fail: no official Docker image exists on Docker Hub or GHCR for `@dbml/cli`, `dbml-renderer`, or the `holistics/dbml` project itself (confirmed by direct registry query); the only images found are unofficial, single-tag, stale (2019/2023) third-party uploads. SVG is possible only via the unofficial third-party `dbml-renderer` CLI; PNG is not documented as an output format anywhere in either toolchain.

Licence/governance: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file, direct read, corroborated by GitHub's own detection); single-vendor governance under Holistics Software Pte Ltd, the same company behind the commercial dbdiagram.io/dbdocs.io products DBML feeds; no GOVERNANCE.md/MAINTAINERS.md. Not at risk of abandonment: near-daily releases through August 2026 (v10.1.1 the same day as retrieval).

Generation/views/DDL: DBML has a real, named, language-level `DiagramView` construct (Tables/Notes/TableGroups/Schemas categories) — the closest analogue among all seven candidates to a Structurizr-style named subset view — but whether any open-source renderer actually honours it when producing an image was not confirmed. No official application-type generator exists (Pydantic/SQLAlchemy); the only lead found, `dbml-builder` on PyPI, is unofficial and unaffiliated. DDL derivation via `dbml2sql` is strong and directly confirmed by the project's own golden-file exporter tests for composite PKs, JSON columns, enums, nullable FKs, and CHECK constraints; self-referencing-FK, multi-column-UNIQUE, and one-to-one-uniqueness survival through DDL generation specifically were not found demonstrated in any examined fixture (a gap, not a confirmed failure).

findings.title: Mermaid erDiagram (incumbent baseline) — construct expressiveness, MUST-criteria, licence, and generation profile
findings.summary:
Ten advanced constructs, verdicts drawn from the erDiagram grammar (erDiagram.jison, erDb.ts) and the official syntax reference, as of Mermaid v11.16.1:
- Composite primary keys: expressible-only-via-workaround — PK is a per-attribute label only; two rows each marked PK render as two independent key flags, with no composite semantic, confirmed at both grammar and documentation level.
- JSON payload columns: expressible — the type token is unstructured free text.
- Enumerated string domains: expressible-only-via-workaround — no enum/domain keyword exists; only an unparsed, unenforced double-quoted comment could carry the value set.
- Several self-referencing FKs on one table: expressible — the grammar/DB layer (`erDb.ts` addRelationship/addEntity) places no restriction on entA===entB or on repeated self-references.
- Nullable FKs: expressible — as of v11.16.0 (2026-06-29), a `?` suffix on the type token marks an attribute optional/nullable — a recent addition.
- Multi-column UNIQUE: expressible-only-via-workaround — UK is a per-attribute label like PK, with no grouping mechanism.
- One-to-zero-or-one: expressible — the documented two-character cardinality markers (`||--o|`) directly support it.
- Value constraint beyond type: expressible-only-via-workaround — only the unparsed comment field could carry it.
- Several logical schemas in one database: not-expressible — no schema/namespace/grouping production exists in the erDiagram grammar (class diagrams have a separate namespace keyword erDiagram does not share).
- Cross-cutting domain_id convention: not-expressible — `erDb.ts` is a pure structure-builder with no rule-evaluation logic; would require an entirely external script against the raw `.mmd` text.

The single most consequential finding for Mermaid as the incumbent under replacement: direct reading of `erDb.ts`'s `addEntity`/`addRelationship` shows that a relationship statement naming a previously undeclared entity is NOT rejected — it is silently auto-vivified into a new, attribute-less entity and rendered as though intentional. Mermaid's ER parser has no semantic-consistency check at all, only lexical/grammatical syntax checking.

Reading the actual in-repo incumbent artifact (docs/spec/supplementary_specs/entity-model.md) confirms this gap is not merely theoretical: only JSON payload columns and the one-to-zero-or-one relationship are fully expressed inside the diagram itself. Enumerated domains, nullable FKs, multi-column UNIQUE, and the value-constraint-beyond-type construct are carried ONLY in prose beneath the diagram — e.g. FOLDER_RUN.execution_context is typed plain 'string' in the diagram, with its SCHEDULED|MANUAL domain stated only in prose. Several logical schemas and the domain_id convention appear nowhere in the artifact, diagram or prose.

MUSTs: (1) plain-text/version-controlled — pass; product-neutral — pass (no dialect-specific typing required). (2) Validator exits non-zero — fail: `mmdc` has no dedicated validate/lint subcommand; the only `process.exit(1)` calls found in `src/index.js` are for CLI-usage mistakes (missing file, wrong extension), not a parse/render failure; and, per the semantic finding above, a semantically inconsistent diagram does not fail at all — it renders 'successfully'. (3) SVG/PNG from an ephemeral Docker container, zero local install — pass: the official `minlag/mermaid-cli` image is actively published and current (pushed 2026-08-03), and SVG/PNG are both documented, first-class `-o` output formats.

Licence/governance: MIT (mermaid core, copyright Knut Sveidqvist; mermaid-cli carries its own, separate MIT copyright, Tyler Long). No GOVERNANCE.md; maintainer-review-plus-named-release-authority (knsv 'in charge of the release process'), neither foundation-governed nor documented as single-vendor-commercial (no company is named as controlling mermaid-js/mermaid core, distinct from the separate commercial 'Mermaid Chart' entity that sponsors some maintainers but is not documented as controlling governance). Freshest-looking candidate by construction, being the incumbent in active use: core pushed 2026-08-14 (day of research), latest release 2026-08-04; mermaid-cli pushed 2026-08-10, latest release 2026-06-29.

Generation/views/DDL: no named-subset-view construct exists for erDiagram. No application-type generation of any kind; DDL derivation not applicable (no generation path exists to build it on).

findings.title: LinkML — construct expressiveness, MUST-criteria, licence, and generation profile
findings.summary:
Ten advanced constructs, verdicts drawn from the LinkML metamodel reference, corroborated by the generator documentation and an issue-tracker search:
- Composite primary keys: expressible-only-via-workaround — a class may declare at most one `identifier`/`key` slot (a documented cap); true composite identity is representable only as a compound `unique_keys` constraint standing in for identity, which the docs explicitly state is 'not merely syntactic sugar for a unique_keys definition'. Corroborated by open issue #3501 showing LinkML's singular-identifier FK-resolution logic has had real defects.
- JSON payload columns: expressible-only-via-workaround — no native opaque-JSON scalar exists; only `range: Any` (meant for polymorphic typed values, not an intentional blob) or `range: string` (loses all structure semantics).
- Enumerated string domains: expressible — a native `enums:`/`permissible_values:` block.
- Several self-referencing FKs on one table: expressible — the general `range` mechanism carries no documented cardinality restriction (inferred from the general rule; no worked three-self-reference example was found).
- Nullable FKs: expressible — `required` defaults to false.
- Multi-column UNIQUE (not PK): expressible — `unique_keys` with `unique_key_slots`.
- One-to-zero-or-one: expressible — a non-required, non-multivalued class-range slot is the standard default encoding.
- Value constraint beyond type: expressible — `any_of`/`equals_string` boolean range-expressions directly match a 'positive integer OR literal ALL' shape, but the documentation itself flags this feature as experimental, with behaviour 'not guaranteed to stay consistent'.
- Several logical schemas in one database: expressible-only-via-workaround — the SQL DDL generator's documented algorithm maps one LinkML schema file to exactly one database schema; four schemas would require four separate schema files and manual DDL assembly, with no single documented command for it.
- Cross-cutting domain_id convention: expressible-only-via-workaround — Mixins let an author compose a shared slot into every class that needs it, but nothing checks, after the fact, that every class in a group actually used the mixin; it is an authoring convention, not an automatically verified invariant, and the eight built-in linkml-lint rules do not cover it.

MUSTs: (1) plain-text YAML, version-controlled, product-neutral — pass (generation targets are chosen separately from the source schema). (2) Validator exits non-zero — expressible-only-via-workaround: two separate tools exist. `linkml-lint` (Schema Linter) has clean, explicitly documented graduated exit codes (0 clean / 1 warnings-only / 2 any errors), directly CI-gatable. `linkml validate` (data/schema-instance validation against the metamodel) offers `--exit-on-first-failure`, but its numeric exit-code contract on failure is not stated in the fetched documentation — a genuine documentation gap. (3) SVG/PNG from an ephemeral Docker container, zero local install — fail: an official `linkml/linkml` Docker Hub image exists and is current (1.11.1, amd64+arm64), but the only diagram generator, `gen-erdiagram`, outputs markdown/mermaid TEXT only — its own documentation states plainly, 'There is currently no way to directly generate PNGs/PDFs/etc from the mermaid code. You can use the mermaid live editor,' an external, non-containerised tool. No SVG path exists either.

Licence/governance: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file, direct read). No GOVERNANCE.md/MAINTAINERS.md was found for LinkML's own repository — a genuine negative finding, not inferred informal governance. A linkml.io how-to guide describes a generic 'Steering Council' governance TEMPLATE for OTHER projects that adopt LinkML (citing Bioschemas, GA4GH, and others), which must not be mistaken for LinkML's own governance. Not at risk of abandonment: v1.11.1 released roughly three months before the August 2026 retrieval date.

Generation/views/DDL: real, documented Pydantic and SQLAlchemy generators exist — LinkML is the only candidate in this survey with two first-party generators, plus a separate SQL DDL generator (gen-sqlddl/SQLTableGenerator), the broadest generation surface found. Construct survival through generation is uneven: composite identity, opaque JSON, multi-column-unique-as-SQL-UNIQUE, and the any_of value constraint are each classified not-expressible for survival specifically, either because the construct never truly exists in LinkML form to survive (composite identity, JSON) or because no generator page documents translating them (unique_keys, any_of); enumerated domains, self-referencing FKs, nullable FKs, and one-to-zero-or-one DO survive per the documented general mapping rules. No named-subset-view/diagram-splitting connection was found — the `subsets`/`in_subset` tagging mechanism exists but is not documented as feeding diagram generation.

findings.title: PlantUML IE/Chen notation — construct expressiveness, MUST-criteria, licence, and generation profile
findings.summary:
Ten advanced constructs, verdicts drawn from the IE-diagram, ER-diagram (Chen), and class-diagram reference pages:
- Composite primary keys: expressible-only-via-workaround — IE notation marks several attributes '*' above the separator; Chen notation marks several attributes individually '<<key>>' or nests sub-attributes; neither is a language-level 'this group of N columns is jointly the key' assertion. A 2021 community forum question asking exactly how to draw a composite-key relation found no documented built-in answer, corroborating the docs' own silence.
- JSON payload columns: expressible — a free-text type label after ':', e.g. 'schedule_spec : json'.
- Enumerated string domains: expressible-only-via-workaround — a real `enum` keyword exists (inherited from class diagrams) but declares a separate UML enumeration element, not a constraint bound to a specific attribute's value set.
- Several self-referencing FKs on one table: expressible — labelled relations with independent multiplicities on each end; nothing restricts an entity from relating to itself multiple times with distinct labels.
- Nullable FKs: expressible — documented crow's-foot 'zero' cardinality markers (`|o--`, `}o--`) are the conventional notation for an optional/nullable referencing side.
- Multi-column UNIQUE (not PK): expressible-only-via-workaround — no dedicated keyword; only a free-text 'note' attached to the entity.
- One-to-zero-or-one: expressible — direct, literal application of the documented crow's-foot symbol set (`||--o|`).
- Value constraint beyond type: expressible-only-via-workaround — no CHECK/value-range grammar; only free text after the attribute name.
- Several logical schemas in one database: expressible-only-via-workaround — the `namespace`/`package` keyword (inherited from class diagrams) provides real dotted-qualified-name scoping, closer to schema-qualification than pure visual grouping, but has no declared connection to database-schema semantics or enforcement.
- Cross-cutting domain_id convention: not-expressible — no construct anywhere in the ER/IE/class-diagram documentation, and the CLI has no lint/rule-assertion option either.

MUSTs: (1) plain-text, version-controlled, product-neutral — pass (the notation requires no dialect-specific typing). (2) Validator exits non-zero — pass on syntax: PlantUML documents an explicit exit-code contract (legacy CLI: -1 on any diagram error; new beta CLI: 0 success / 50 no file / 100 no diagram / 200 syntax errors), plus a `--check-syntax` flag for validation without rendering — the most explicit, primary-sourced exit-code documentation found across all seven candidates. Semantic validation beyond syntax, however, is not-expressible: no flag or documented behaviour checks referential integrity or duplicate attributes, and whether a relation referencing a previously undeclared entity is silently auto-created (well known for PlantUML class diagrams generally) or rejected was NOT confirmed against a primary source specific to ER/IE diagrams within this survey — recorded as an unresolved gap, not a cited fact. (3) SVG/PNG from an ephemeral Docker container, zero local install — pass: official `plantuml/plantuml` and `plantuml/plantuml-server` images are confirmed current on Docker Hub (pushed 2026-06-08, tied to the v1.2026.6 release); the Dockerfile's ENTRYPOINT runs the jar directly, and `--svg`/`--png` are documented, first-class CLI flags including a piped stdin/stdout mode.

Licence/governance: multi-license, not a single SPDX identifier — GPL-3.0-or-later is the root/default LICENSE, with the identical source additionally offered, at the licensee's option, under GPL-2.0, LGPL-3.0, Apache-2.0, BSD-3-Clause, EPL-1.0, or MIT via dedicated subprojects (LICENSES.md, the project's own authoritative statement). GitHub's own repository-metadata auto-detection reports the SPDX field as 'LGPL-3.0' — this directly contradicts the actual root LICENSE file (full GPL-3.0-or-later text). Generated diagram output (SVG/PNG) is explicitly stated NOT to be covered by the GPL and usable without attribution. Governance: single-named-copyright-holder (Arnaud Roques, 2009-2026), no foundation/steering-committee, a standard PR/issue workflow — recorded as single-maintainer/BDFL-style, with an unexplored bus-factor question. Not at risk of abandonment: latest tagged release v1.2026.6 (2026-06-08), latest push 2026-08-12.

Generation/views/DDL: a real, documented named-subset TEXT-inclusion mechanism exists (`!startsub`/`!endsub`/`!includesub`), but it operates on author-tagged line ranges, not model-aware entity/relationship selection — a workaround relative to a Structurizr-style view. No application-type generation of any kind was found, a clean negative corroborated by both the exhaustive Output Format table (all ten formats are diagram/image/markup, none application source code) and zero GitHub code/issue hits for 'pydantic'/'sqlalchemy' in the repository. DDL derivation is therefore not-applicable (no generation pipeline exists to derive it from).

findings.title: Prisma schema language — construct expressiveness, MUST-criteria, licence, and generation profile
findings.summary:
Ten advanced constructs, verdicts drawn from the Prisma Schema Reference and the Database Features Matrix:
- Composite primary keys: expressible — `@@id([field1, field2])`, documented for every non-MongoDB provider ('The MongoDB connector does not support composite IDs').
- JSON payload columns: expressible — the native `Json` scalar, documented for PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQLite(6.2.0+)/MongoDB/CockroachDB; explicitly NOT supported on SQL Server ('Microsoft SQL Server does not have a specific data type for JSON') — a provider-conditional gap.
- Enumerated string domains: expressible — a native `enum` block; explicitly NOT supported on Microsoft SQL Server — another provider-conditional gap.
- Several self-referencing FKs on one table: expressible — the documentation explicitly covers multiple simultaneous self-relations on one model, disambiguated by distinct `@relation("Name")` strings on both sides, with no stated limit on count.
- Nullable FKs: expressible — the `?` type modifier on the relation scalar field.
- Multi-column UNIQUE: expressible — `@@unique([field1, field2])`, independent of `@@id`, provided all fields are mandatory.
- One-to-zero-or-one: expressible — an optional relation scalar plus an optional relation field on the '1' side.
- Value constraint beyond type: not-expressible — the Database Features Matrix states plainly the CHECK constraint has no Prisma-schema representation ('Not yet') and no Prisma-Migrate generation path either; corroborated independently by open GitHub issue prisma/prisma#3388 ('Support SQL Check constraints', opened December 2019, still open), which states outright 'there is no way of expressing SQL check constraints in the Prisma schema.'
- Several logical schemas in one database: expressible-only-via-workaround — the `multiSchema` preview/GA feature (GA since 6.13.0) supports this only on PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, and SQL Server; it is unavailable on SQLite and MySQL.
- Cross-cutting domain_id convention: not-expressible — no lint/rule mechanism exists in `prisma validate`, `format`, or any listed subcommand; would require a custom script against the schema AST or the generated DMMF, entirely outside Prisma's own validator.

Product neutrality (part of MUST 1): fails on a strict reading — a `.prisma` file cannot be written without exactly one non-optional `provider` chosen from a closed six-value enum (postgresql/mysql/sqlite/sqlserver/mongodb/cockroachdb); there is no 'unset'/generic value documented anywhere, so authoring a valid schema.prisma is itself an act of picking a database product, and several advanced constructs (multiSchema, enum, Json) are themselves provider-conditional on top of that.

MUSTs 2-3: (2) validator exits non-zero — expressible-only-via-workaround: `prisma validate` and `prisma format --check` are documented to detect errors (a distinct 'Error code', e.g. P1012, and an error count on failure) and `format --check` is explicitly framed for CI use, but neither page states a numeric exit-code contract outright — inferred, not a confirmed first-party guarantee. (3) SVG/PNG from an ephemeral Docker container, zero local install — fail: no official Prisma Docker image exists (the only Docker-Hub image plausibly named for the product, `prismagraphql/prisma`, is the deprecated Prisma-1 GraphQL-server product, unmaintained since 2019; the officially recommended Docker path is to build a custom Dockerfile FROM a generic node base image and run `npx prisma` inside it); SVG/PNG are available only via the unofficial third-party `prisma-erd-generator`, which itself depends on `@mermaid-js/mermaid-cli` plus Puppeteer — a third-party-on-third-party chain inheriting Mermaid's own renderer limitations, and whose own README frames that dependency chain as a recurring source of cross-platform breakage.

Licence/governance: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file, direct read, corroborated by GitHub API). Single-vendor, commercially-backed open source: the repository is owned by Prisma Data, Inc., named venture-capital investors are disclosed on the company's own About page, and there is no GOVERNANCE.md (confirmed 404). A load-bearing nuance: the actively-committed default branch is 'Prisma Next', explicitly documented as pre-1.0 with breaking changes expected between minor versions; CONTRIBUTING.md itself names the separately-branched 'Prisma 7' as 'the recommended path for production today.' Not at risk of abandonment by either release-recency (v8.0.0-rc.1, 2026-08-07) or activity-recency (commit the same day as retrieval) tests.

Generation/views/DDL: no first-party named-subset-view mechanism; the third-party `prisma-erd-generator`'s filtering flags (`ignorePattern`, `ignoreEnums`, `ignoreViews`) can approximate one only via multiple differently-configured generator blocks in the same schema — a workaround, not a documented feature. Python application-type generation exists only via the third-party `prisma-client-py`, which GitHub's own API reports as archived and whose README states outright 'is no longer being maintained' — a first-party admission, not external inference; per-construct survival of the advanced constructs through this generator was never tested. DDL derivation IS first-party and real (`prisma migrate diff --script`), provider-bound and only partially supported for MongoDB; construct-by-construct DDL fidelity beyond what is already known absent from the schema (the CHECK constraint) was not independently tested.

findings.title: Atlas HCL (ariga.io) — construct expressiveness, MUST-criteria, licence, and generation profile
findings.summary:
Ten advanced constructs, verdicts drawn from the Atlas HCL schema-language and column-types reference, corroborated and complicated by a GitHub-API-based contrary-evidence search:
- Composite primary keys: expressible — `primary_key { columns = [...] }`, list-typed with no documented cardinality limit (inferred from grammar shape, no literal 2+-column worked example). Corroborated at the operational layer by two closed issues describing real historical migration-planner bugs around composite keys and one still-open issue (#2086, UNIQUE-constraint rename ordering); authoring-time expressibility is not disputed, but migration-execution has a real bug history.
- JSON payload columns: expressible-only-via-workaround — `json`/`jsonb` types exist per dialect, but the exact type name is dialect-specific (part of the broader product-neutrality leak below).
- Enumerated string domains: expressible, but not one construct — MySQL uses an inline `enum` type while PostgreSQL requires a separately declared top-level `enum` schema object bound via `type = enum.<name>`, a dialect-divergent shape. One closed issue (#2252) shows PostgreSQL enum value reordering/replacement is explicitly 'not supported' by Atlas's migration flow — a gap between authoring and evolving the construct.
- Several self-referencing FKs on one table: expressible — each `foreign_key` block is an independently named, repeatable child resource; a documented single self-reference example plus the general repeatable-block pattern support three simultaneous self-refs (extrapolated, no 3-at-once worked example). A targeted GitHub Search API query for 'self reference' foreign key returned zero results — an explicit non-finding, not a confirmation.
- Nullable FKs: expressible — the ordinary column `null` attribute applies to FK-bearing columns; a targeted search also returned zero relevant issues (explicit non-finding).
- Multi-column UNIQUE: expressible — `index { unique = true columns = [...] }`, the same list-typed pattern as primary_key.
- One-to-zero-or-one: expressible-only-via-workaround — no relationship/cardinality keyword exists anywhere in the HCL reference; must be reconstructed from a nullable FK column plus a unique index on it.
- Value constraint beyond type: expressible-only-via-workaround — a `check { expr = "..." }` block exists, but `expr` is raw, dialect-specific SQL text (the documented PostgreSQL domain example uses the Postgres-only `~` operator and `VALUE` keyword). A merged 2022 PR specifically rejects CHECK constraints unsupported by the target MySQL version/config — good gate behaviour, but direct evidence the construct's actual acceptance is dialect- and version-dependent, not uniform.
- Several logical schemas in one database: expressible — multiple `schema` blocks with Table-Qualification syntax and a documented cross-schema FK reference form. BUT two open GitHub issues complicate this: #1584 (a multi-schema `apply` silently reports 'no changes' despite a genuine diff, open since 2023) and #2957 (same-named tables across schema files collide with 'multiple reference tables found' unless every table uses the qualified form) — directly relevant to Gigacron's configuration/runtime/audit/resources split, which is exactly this collision scenario.
- Cross-cutting domain_id convention: expressible-only-via-workaround — Atlas ships a purpose-built Schema Rule language for exactly this class of policy, a genuine built-in mechanism in kind, but it is licensed exclusively to Pro/Enterprise accounts per two independent, non-conflicting official pages, so a free/Community-tier project cannot use it. This construct's issue-tracker search, along with the one-to-zero-or-one construct, was NEVER queried at all — no plausible search vocabulary was identified for either — and is recorded as UNEXECUTED, not as 'nothing found'.

MUSTs: (1) plain-text HCL, version-controlled — pass; product-neutral — expressible-only-via-workaround / partial: structural keywords are dialect-neutral, but column TYPE NAMES, ENUM DECLARATION SHAPE, and CHECK EXPRESSION SYNTAX all diverge per dialect, and `schema lint`/`schema apply` require a live 'dev database' (an ephemeral Docker container via `docker://<engine>/<version>/<name>`, but one committing the validator's own runtime to a specific engine and version) — extending the dialect leak to the validator's runtime-dependency level. (2) Validator exits non-zero — expressible-only-via-workaround: `atlas schema validate` is documented only in prose ('returns an error'); the sole primary-source passage with an explicit numeric 'exit code 1' statement is scoped to `atlas migrate lint`'s destructive-change analyzer, not `schema validate`/`schema lint` by name. (3) SVG/PNG from an ephemeral Docker container, zero local install — fail for the visualization capability specifically: the official `arigaio/atlas` Docker image is confirmed current and actively published, but every documented description of Atlas's ERD/visualization capability routes through Atlas Cloud (the public `gh.atlasgo.cloud` 'Explore' page or a login-gated personal workspace) — no local SVG/PNG file-export flag was found in any primary source checked. DDL derivation (`schema apply --dry-run`), separately, IS a genuine local, container-runnable capability.

Licence/governance: a genuinely three-tier structure — (1) the repository's LICENSE file is Apache-2.0 for a distinct 'Community Edition' build; (2) the standard/default distribution most users actually run is licensed under a separate 'Atlas MSA' — free to download but NOT Apache-2.0, with additional proprietary features and a wider database-driver list; (3) 'Atlas Pro'/'Enterprise' is a further paid subscription tier gating the custom Schema Rule language needed for domain_id (confirmed Pro-only by two non-conflicting official pages) and, per two DIRECTLY CONTRADICTING official pages (atlasgo.io/features: 'Schema Visualization — Pro Plan Only' vs atlasgo.io/pricing: 'ERD visualization' listed under the free Starter tier), possibly the visualization feature as well — this contradiction between two first-party Ariga pages is recorded as unresolved. No GOVERNANCE.md/MAINTAINERS.md; single-vendor (Ariga, Inc.). Not at risk of abandonment: latest release v1.3.0 (2026-08-02), latest commit 2026-07-29 — though a genuine, unresolved discrepancy exists between two Atlas source records: the Docker registry facet observed a '1.3.1' tag with an estimated push date of 2026-08-13, one day ahead of the latest tag (v1.3.0) the GitHub API itself reports; not resolved here.

Generation/views/DDL: no named/reusable view construct — the closest mechanism is ad hoc re-running `inspect`/`validate`/`apply` with different `--schema`/`--include`/`--exclude` flags, reconstructed each time. No Python/application-type generation in the HCL-to-code direction — the only documented SQLAlchemy integration runs the opposite direction. DDL derivation is a genuine, first-party, strong capability.

findings.title: D2 with SQL table shapes — construct expressiveness, MUST-criteria, licence, and generation profile
findings.summary:
Ten advanced constructs, verdicts drawn from the D2 'SQL Tables' documentation and its embedded examples:
- Composite primary keys: not-expressible — the `constraint` field is declared per single row/column only; the documented array syntax (`constraint: [primary_key; unique]`) applies MULTIPLE constraint LABELS to ONE column, not one constraint spanning multiple columns. Directly and explicitly confirmed by the maintainers' own still-open feature request (d2lang/d2#671, opened 2023-01-16): 'At the moment d2 can't represent FKs that are composed of more than one column,' with the reporter's own example showing no available syntax for a joint `(id, tenant)` key — the one construct across this entire survey confirmed not-expressible by an explicit, first-party maintainer statement rather than by absence-of-mention.
- JSON payload columns: expressible-only-via-workaround — the row's type slot is free text (the official example uses `jsonb`), but D2 attaches no semantics to it whatsoever, identical in kind to the same example set's use of the non-standard, nonsense type `blob` without complaint.
- Enumerated string domains: not-expressible — the row grammar has exactly two free-text slots (type, constraint) and no enum/domain mechanism.
- Several self-referencing FKs on one table: expressible-only-via-workaround — the connection syntax (`table.col -> table.col`) places no restriction on source and target table being different, so three self-referencing connections CAN be drawn, but each connection is a generic D2 edge with no FK-specific semantics.
- Nullable FKs: not-expressible — no documented constraint keyword for nullability at all (only `primary_key`/`foreign_key`/`unique` are recognised).
- Multi-column UNIQUE (not PK): not-expressible — the same structural gap as composite PK; corroborated by the same open issue #671 plus sibling issues #672/#1386 describing the constraint model as a simple per-column label list.
- One-to-zero-or-one: expressible-only-via-workaround — documented crow's-foot-style arrowheads can be applied to a connection to make it LOOK like a cardinality constraint, but arrowhead choice is purely a rendering/styling attribute, not interpreted by the compiler as an enforced or checked cardinality.
- Value constraint beyond type: not-expressible — no CHECK/value-expression grammar anywhere in the row model.
- Several logical schemas in one database: expressible-only-via-workaround — D2's generic `container` primitive can visually nest sql_table shapes into groups resembling four schemas, but the documentation attaches no schema-specific semantics to this; no schema-qualified naming or schema-level constraint exists, and the FAQ confirms a shape belongs to exactly one container with no near-term plan to change that.
- Cross-cutting domain_id convention: not-expressible — `d2 validate` performs syntax parsing only (confirmed by direct Go source reading, see MUSTs below); no lint, plugin, or custom-rule-authoring mechanism was found in the documentation or the issue tracker.

MUSTs: (1) plain-text, version-controlled, product-neutral — pass (free-text type/constraint slots require no dialect-specific keywords), though this neutrality is largely a byproduct of the shape enforcing no real semantics rather than genuine dialect abstraction. (2) Validator exits non-zero — expressible, and the best source-confirmed of all seven candidates: direct reading of `d2cli/validate.go` and the shared `xmain.go` library shows any error from `validateCmd` propagates to `mainFatal`, which calls `os.Exit(code)` (default 1). `validate` calls only `d2lib.Parse` (pure syntax/AST parsing), never `d2compiler.Compile` (the semantic-resolution path used only by the render command), so semantic-level issues are not caught by `validate` specifically — and D2 has no 'undeclared shape' error CLASS at all by design, since connection syntax auto-declares any shape it references. The specific semantic test case this survey probed for (an undeclared-entity reference) is therefore moot for D2, not merely uncaught. (3) SVG/PNG from an ephemeral Docker container, zero local install — expressible with an open caveat: the official `terrastruct/d2` (renamed `d2lang/d2`) image is confirmed current on Docker Hub; SVG export is native and dependency-free (D2's own renderer, the CLI's default format); PNG (and PDF/PPTX, built from PNG) depends on Playwright spinning up a headless Chromium browser — whether the official Docker image bundles this pre-installed or triggers an on-the-fly download at first PNG-export time was NOT confirmed by any source consulted.

Licence/governance: Mozilla Public License 2.0 for D2 itself (LICENSE.txt, direct read) — distinct from and NOT the same as the optional, proprietary, closed-source 'TALA' layout engine, which the project's own docs describe plainly as 'Not free.' D2 functions fully without TALA (the default Dagre layout and the open-source ELK layout engine are both included and open), and the one FK-related capability mentioned as tied to TALA — connections pointing to the exact row — is also available via the open-source ELK engine per the same documentation sentence, so TALA is an optional accuracy upgrade, not a MUST-relevant paid gate. No GOVERNANCE.md/MAINTAINERS.md; single-vendor (Terrastruct Inc., which also sells TALA). Not at risk of abandonment: most recent commit 2026-08-12, though the most recent tagged release (v0.7.1) is a year old (2025-08-19) — a real release/activity gap worth naming even though it does not, on its own, trigger the brief's both-stale abandonment flag.

Generation/views/DDL: `Layers`/`Scenarios`/`Steps` produce multiple named 'boards' from one source file, but their documented purpose is overlay/abstraction-level (a Layer starts as a BLANK board; a Scenario inherits the base plus/minus explicit modifications), not subset SELECTION of an existing large model — a workaround relative to a Structurizr-style named view. No application-type generation of any kind was found, corroborated by both official-docs silence and a zero-hit GitHub issue-tracker search for pydantic/sqlalchemy/dataclass/'generate types'. DDL derivation is therefore not-applicable.

findings.title: Language expressiveness and toolchain maturity move independently, and pull in opposite directions for different candidates
findings.summary: The recorded evidence shows expressiveness and tooling maturity are not correlated across candidates. Atlas HCL: rich language (composite PKs, self-referencing FKs, multi-schema) with a real Docker-published validator, but ERD visualization is cloud-only and the custom schema-rule engine needed for the domain_id convention is Pro/Enterprise-paid — strong language, partly gated tooling. LinkML: the richest construct coverage of any YAML-based candidate plus the only two first-party Pydantic and SQLAlchemy generators found in this survey, yet its own diagram generator explicitly cannot produce SVG/PNG at all — strong language and generation, absent rendering. DBML: rich language including a genuine named-view construct (DiagramView), yet the official CLI's own source code has no non-zero exit on a compiler error and no official Docker image exists anywhere — strong language, weak/absent packaging. Mermaid: a thin language — no composite keys, no enums, no schemas, no cross-cutting rules — paired with the most mature, actively-published Docker tooling in the survey and reliable SVG/PNG, but zero semantic validation, so mature tooling sits on top of a language that cannot express or check what Gigacron needs. PlantUML: a moderate, workaround-heavy language paired with the most explicit, primary-sourced numeric exit-code contract found in this survey and solid native Docker SVG/PNG, but zero application-type generation of any kind. Prisma: strong construct coverage for most constructs paired with a completely absent official Docker image and an archived, self-declared-unmaintained third-party Python generator — strong language, largely absent official packaging outside the JS/TS ecosystem. D2: almost no real relational semantics in its sql_table shape — composite PK and multi-column UNIQUE are not-expressible even via workaround, confirmed by the maintainers' own open issue — paired with the most rigorously source-confirmed non-zero-exit validator behaviour in the survey and dependency-free native SVG export. On the evidence gathered, none of the seven candidates combines strong construct expressiveness, a confirmed CI-gatable validator, and confirmed zero-local-install SVG-plus-PNG rendering all at once.

findings.title: Pass/fail against the brief's three MUST criteria, by candidate
findings.summary:
MUST 1 (plain-text, version-controlled, product-neutral source of truth): pass for DBML, Mermaid, LinkML, PlantUML, and D2. Partial/fail for Atlas HCL — structural keywords are dialect-neutral but column type names, enum declaration shape, and CHECK expression syntax all diverge per dialect, and validation requires a live dev-database tied to one engine. Fail for Prisma — a `.prisma` file cannot be written without choosing exactly one provider from a closed enum; there is no product-neutral/unset option.

MUST 2 (validator exits non-zero on a malformed or internally inconsistent model): fail for DBML (no `process.exit` on a compiler error, confirmed by source reading) and for Mermaid (no dedicated validator at all, and a semantically inconsistent diagram — an undeclared-entity reference — renders successfully rather than failing). Expressible-only-via-workaround for LinkML (use `linkml-lint` specifically, which has documented exit codes; `linkml validate`'s own exit-code contract is undocumented), Prisma (documented error output and CI framing, but no explicit numeric exit-code contract), and Atlas HCL (the only explicit 'exit code 1' statement found is scoped to `migrate lint`'s destructive-change analyzer, not `schema validate`/`schema lint`). Pass for PlantUML on syntax errors specifically (an explicit, documented 0/50/100/200 or -1 exit-code contract), though semantic validation beyond syntax is unconfirmed. Best source-confirmed pass is D2 — direct Go source reading confirms `os.Exit(code)` on any validate error — though `validate` itself is syntax-only and D2 has no 'undeclared shape' error class by design.

MUST 3 (SVG and PNG rendering from an ephemeral Docker container with zero local install): pass for Mermaid and PlantUML, both with official, actively published Docker images and documented native SVG+PNG CLI flags. Fail for DBML (no official Docker image anywhere) and Prisma (no official Docker image; the officially recommended path is a hand-built Dockerfile around a generic node base image). Fail for LinkML (an official Docker image exists, but its only diagram generator cannot produce SVG or PNG at all, only markdown/mermaid text). Fail for Atlas HCL specifically for the visualization capability (the image itself is available and current, but ERD viewing routes through Atlas Cloud, not a local file export) while DDL derivation from the same image is a genuine local capability. Open/unconfirmed for D2 — the official image is current and SVG is native and dependency-free, but whether PNG's Playwright/Chromium dependency ships pre-installed in the image or downloads on first use was not confirmed by any source.

On this evidence, no surveyed candidate passes all three MUSTs cleanly.

findings.title: Licence and governance: free-core/paid-tier splits, and one confirmed metadata-vs-LICENSE contradiction
findings.summary:
Atlas HCL: a three-tier licensing structure — an Apache-2.0 'Community Edition', a free-but-proprietary 'Atlas MSA' standard distribution, and a paid Pro/Enterprise tier. The custom Schema Rule language needed for the domain_id convention is confirmed Pro/Enterprise-only by two non-conflicting official pages, and ERD visualization's tier status is the subject of a direct, unresolved contradiction between two official Ariga pages (atlasgo.io/features states Pro-only; atlasgo.io/pricing lists it under the free Starter tier).

PlantUML: repository metadata (GitHub API's auto-detected SPDX field, 'LGPL-3.0') directly contradicts the actual root LICENSE file (full GPL-3.0-or-later text) and the project's own authoritative LICENSES.md (multi-license, GPL-3.0-or-later default) — the one clean instance in this survey of repository metadata disagreeing with the actual LICENSE file.

D2: an MPL-2.0 open core plus an optional, explicitly 'Not free' proprietary layout engine (TALA) that is not required for any MUST-relevant capability, since the open-source ELK engine provides the same row-level FK routing accuracy documented as a TALA benefit.

Prisma: fully Apache-2.0, but single-vendor commercially-backed governance with no foundation, and a documented nuance where the actively-committed default branch is a pre-1.0 rewrite while the production-recommended version lives on a separate branch.

DBML, Mermaid, and LinkML: each fully open (Apache-2.0/MIT/Apache-2.0 respectively) with no paid tier found, and each lacking a formal governance charter (GOVERNANCE.md/MAINTAINERS.md), resting on single-vendor maintainer-led (DBML: Holistics Software; Mermaid: informal, no company documented for the core project) or unclear (LinkML: no charter for its own repository, and a same-domain how-to guide about OTHER projects' governance that could be mistaken for LinkML's own) patterns.

findings.title: Named subset views, application-type generation, and DDL derivation, across candidates
findings.summary:
Named subset views comparable to Structurizr's: DBML's `DiagramView` (Tables/Notes/TableGroups/Schemas categories) is the only genuinely model-aware, named-view language construct found in the survey, though whether any open-source renderer honours it is unconfirmed. D2's Layers/Scenarios/Steps and PlantUML's `!includesub` are real but workaround-level (overlay/abstraction-level or text-line-range mechanisms, not subset selection over an existing model). Atlas offers only ad hoc `--schema`/`--include`/`--exclude` re-runs, not a saved artefact. LinkML's `subsets`/`in_subset` tagging is not documented as connected to diagram generation at all. Mermaid and Prisma have no first-party mechanism at all (Prisma's third-party `prisma-erd-generator` offers filtering flags as a workaround).

Application-type generation: LinkML is the only candidate with two first-party, actively-documented generators (Pydantic and SQLAlchemy) plus a separate SQL DDL generator — the broadest generation surface in the survey — but construct survival through generation is uneven (composite identity, opaque JSON, multi-column-unique-as-UNIQUE, and the any_of value constraint are each not confirmed to survive; enums, self-referencing FKs, nullable FKs, and one-to-zero-or-one are). DBML, PlantUML, D2, and Atlas have no first-party application-type generator at all; DBML and Prisma each have an unofficial third-party option (dbml-builder and prisma-client-py respectively), the latter explicitly self-declared no-longer-maintained.

DDL derivation: strong and first-party for Atlas (`schema apply --dry-run`), DBML (`dbml2sql`, confirmed by golden-file tests for five of ten constructs, unconfirmed for three), and Prisma (`migrate diff --script`, provider-bound, MongoDB-partial). LinkML's DDL generator exists but shares the same construct-survival gaps as its other generators. Not-applicable for PlantUML and D2, since neither has any generation pipeline to derive DDL from. Mermaid has no generation of any kind.

findings.title: Release and repository activity: no surveyed candidate is flagged at risk of abandonment, with one release/activity gap worth naming
findings.summary: All seven candidates show either a tagged release or repository activity within the 18 months before August 2026 (since roughly February 2025). DBML: near-daily releases through August 2026 (v10.1.1 the same day as retrieval). Mermaid: core pushed 2026-08-14 (day of retrieval), latest release 2026-08-04; mermaid-cli pushed 2026-08-10, latest release 2026-06-29. LinkML: v1.11.1 released 2026-05-20, roughly three months before retrieval. PlantUML: latest release v1.2026.6 (2026-06-08), most recent push 2026-08-12. Prisma: latest commit 2026-08-14 (day of retrieval), latest prerelease v8.0.0-rc.1 2026-08-07, with the noted caveat that this activity sits partly on a pre-1.0 rewrite branch rather than solely incremental maintenance of the production-recommended v7. Atlas: latest release v1.3.0 (2026-08-02), latest commit 2026-07-29, with an unresolved cross-record discrepancy where the Docker registry shows an apparent '1.3.1' tag one day ahead of the latest tag the GitHub API itself reports. D2: latest commit 2026-08-12 (four days before retrieval), but the latest TAGGED release is a full year earlier (2025-08-19) — the one candidate in the survey where release recency and activity recency diverge this widely; still inside the freshness window on the activity measure alone, so not flagged, but worth naming as a distinct pattern from the other six candidates' more tightly coupled release/activity cadence.

uncertainties: Atlas HCL: two official Ariga pages directly contradict each other on whether Schema Visualization is Pro-plan-only (atlasgo.io/features) or included in the free Starter tier (atlasgo.io/pricing); neither page is dated, both are equally official, and no third page was found to arbitrate. This survey records the contradiction without resolving it.

PlantUML: GitHub's own repository-metadata auto-detected SPDX licence field ('LGPL-3.0') contradicts the actual root LICENSE file (full GPL-3.0-or-later text) and the project's own authoritative LICENSES.md. This survey treats LICENSES.md as authoritative but the contradiction itself remains an unresolved discrepancy in the source base.

Atlas HCL: a Docker Hub tag '1.3.1' with an estimated push date one day ahead of the latest tag (v1.3.0) reported by the GitHub Releases/Tags API is an unresolved discrepancy between two Atlas source records — possibly a Docker-only patch build ahead of its source tag, possibly an artefact of Docker Hub's relative-date display.

Several 'expressible' verdicts for multi-attribute constructs (composite primary keys and multi-column indexes for Atlas HCL; three-simultaneous-self-referencing foreign keys for both DBML and Atlas HCL) are extrapolated from a general grammar rule or a smaller worked example (e.g. a two-column or two-table case), not from a literal worked example matching Gigacron's exact cardinality. These are recorded as expressible on the strength of the general rule, but are less directly demonstrated than constructs with a literal matching example.

Whether PlantUML's well-known class-diagram behaviour of auto-creating an empty entity for an undeclared reference also applies, unmodified, to its ER/IE notation specifically was not confirmed against a primary source dedicated to ER/IE diagrams — it is assumed by extension from general PlantUML familiarity, not cited from an ER/IE-specific page.

D2: whether the official Docker image bundles Playwright/Chromium pre-installed for PNG export, or triggers an on-the-fly dependency download at first invocation, was not confirmed by any source consulted — this bears directly on whether D2's PNG export genuinely meets the zero-local-install requirement inside a container.

DBML: whether any open-source SVG renderer (dbml-renderer) actually honours the documented `DiagramView` filter when producing an image was not confirmed — the language-level construct is documented, but its enforcement in the one third-party rendering path found is unverified.
evidence_gaps: Atlas HCL: the domain_id cross-cutting convention and the one-to-zero-or-one relationship were never queried against the GitHub issue tracker at all, because no plausible search vocabulary was identified for either — this is an UNEXECUTED search, explicitly distinct from a search that ran and found nothing.

LinkML's contrary-evidence search used the general WebSearch tool rather than the authenticated GitHub Issues API; the LinkML source record itself flags this as a weaker method and recommends the API-based approach Atlas's, DBML's, and part of Prisma's searches actually used — LinkML's 'not found' results therefore carry less weight than the API-based searches for other candidates.
LinkML's SQL DDL generator's enum-rendering mechanism (a native CHECK constraint vs. a separate lookup table) was not confirmed by any fetched generator documentation page.
LinkML's `unique_keys` → SQL UNIQUE constraint emission by the SQL DDL generator was not confirmed by any fetched generator documentation page.

DBML: three specific DDL-derivation claims — self-referencing foreign key, multi-column UNIQUE, and one-to-one-with-uniqueness — were not found demonstrated in any examined golden-file exporter-test fixture; recorded as unconfirmed, not as a failure.
Prisma: no documented hard limit on the number of named self-relations a single model may declare was found; absence of a stated limit is not proof no limit exists.
Prisma: construct-by-construct DDL fidelity through `prisma migrate diff --script`, beyond the CHECK-constraint gap already known to be absent upstream in the schema, was not independently tested.

D2 and Atlas HCL: neither project's GHCR (ghcr.io) mirror, if any exists, was exhaustively confirmed; Docker Hub alone was sufficient to answer the availability question for both, so a GHCR listing is an unexplored angle rather than a confirmed absence for either candidate.
limitations: No candidate was installed, executed, or rendered as part of this survey. Every capability, exit-code, and generation-fidelity finding in this report rests on documentary evidence — official documentation, source-code reading, golden-file test fixtures, and public registry-API listings — not on an observed process run. Exit-code and rendering behaviour are documented-but-unverified throughout.

The mandatory contrary-evidence search was executed with materially different rigor across candidates. Atlas HCL's, DBML's, and part of Prisma's searches queried the GitHub Search API directly, an authoritative and reproducible method. LinkML's own contrary-evidence record explicitly flags that it used the general WebSearch tool instead and recommends the API-based method as a stronger follow-up. Apparent 'nothing found' results therefore carry different evidentiary weight depending on which candidate and which method produced them.

Several Mermaid source records (grammar, syntax, tooling) internally cite a 'source-mermaid-erd-contrary-evidence.json' record — for example, GitHub issues #3582 and #4429, and a predecessor-repository issue mermaidjs/mermaid.cli#77 — that does not exist in docs/research/data-modeling-dsl/sources/, confirmed by direct directory listing. This synthesis does not cite that non-existent file and does not treat those specific issue numbers as independently verified evidence in this report; the underlying claims they were meant to support (no composite-key grouping construct, no NOT NULL keyword, historical non-exit-on-error behaviour in a predecessor CLI) are instead corroborated here only through the grammar and source-code readings in source-mermaid-erd-grammar.json and source-mermaid-erd-tooling.json.

Per the dispatching instructions for this synthesis, Atlas HCL's licence-governance and contrary-evidence source records were produced by a separate backfill research dispatch after a session interruption. This synthesis checked their content for internal consistency with the other five Atlas HCL facet records but did not independently verify the backfill dispatch's own provenance.

Freshness and activity dates reflect each source record's own retrieval date (predominantly 2026-08-14, with some component documentation pages last substantively edited as early as 2024-02-01) and will drift from the date of any future re-reading of this report.

Several source records substitute their own retrieval date for a genuine page 'last-updated' date where the underlying documentation carried no visible revision date; this is flagged individually within the affected records and affects the precision, not the substance, of the findings drawn from them.

Docker registry queries in several records (e.g. Atlas HCL, PlantUML) retrieved only the first page of tags (up to 25) rather than the full historical tag inventory; this is sufficient to establish current availability and freshness but not a complete version history.
candidates_for_deeper_falsification_stud: DBML: run @dbml/cli's dbml2sql against a schema modeled on Gigacron's actual composite keys, self-referencing FKs, multi-column UNIQUE, and one-to-one relationships, and inspect whether the generated DDL preserves each construct as the golden-file fixtures suggest but do not directly confirm for these specific cases; also confirm whether the open-source dbml-renderer actually honours the documented DiagramView construct, and whether a wrapper script reading @dbml/core's parsed model can reliably produce a non-zero CI exit code.

Atlas HCL: author Gigacron's four-schema split in Atlas HCL and run `atlas schema apply --dry-run` against a real ephemeral Docker dev-database to see whether the 'several logical schemas' mechanism applies cleanly given the two open GitHub issues (#1584, #2957) describing silent no-ops and table-name collisions; also confirm exactly which capabilities remain available at the free/Community-Edition tier versus require an Atlas Pro/Enterprise login, given the direct contradiction found between atlasgo.io/features and atlasgo.io/pricing on ERD visualization gating.

LinkML: run gen-sqlddl and the Pydantic/SQLAlchemy generators against a schema modeling Gigacron's composite identity, JSON payload columns, and the resource_task_weight any_of value constraint, to determine whether these constructs actually survive generation as this survey's documentary evidence suggests they do not, or whether the documentation is simply incomplete on this point.

PlantUML IE/Chen: feed a diagram referencing an undeclared entity into both the legacy and new command-line interfaces to confirm, at last, whether PlantUML auto-creates an empty box or rejects it for ER/IE diagrams specifically, since no primary source for this behaviour was found despite it being the single most consequential unresolved question for PlantUML's viability as a CI-gate validator.

Prisma: run `prisma validate` and `prisma format --check` against a deliberately malformed schema.prisma to observe the actual exit code, never confirmed as an explicit numeric contract in the documentation, and run `prisma migrate diff --script` against a schema containing Gigacron's advanced constructs to see which actually survive into derived DDL.

D2: run `d2 validate` and a full render against a Gigacron-shaped sql_table model to confirm the documented os.Exit(1)-on-error behaviour in practice, and pull the official terrastruct/d2 (d2lang/d2) Docker image and attempt a PNG export with no prior local Playwright installation, to settle whether the image bundles Chromium or triggers an on-the-fly download that would break a zero-local-install CI gate.

Mermaid erDiagram (incumbent baseline): feed mmdc a diagram with a relationship referencing an undeclared entity to confirm, by direct observation, that it renders successfully with exit code 0 rather than failing — the single most consequential finding this survey uncovered against the incumbent, currently resting on source-code reading (erDb.ts) rather than an observed process exit.
